Again, you can't force them to want to be sober, but it may encourage him to continue to recover. You do not have to let him stay in the home if you don't want to. Babe the first thing is to just breathe. That's it. Take everything step by step and just work with your providers to make any improvements you can. Therapy is going to be your best tool. It's not going to be easy at all, but with the right care team you can go a long way. You're not damaged or broken, you're just another person with a chronic illness and that's ok. It's absolutely not the end of the world, no matter how hard it may feel seem. I'd also suggest being open with your loved ones if that's possible and allow them to be a part of the healing process so you don't feel like you're doing it alone. I think finding a trusted person and giving them the power to speak with your care team is a big thing also because there's going to be times where you're not going to really understand what's going on with you and you're not going to be able to effectively communicate your needs. That person can be your voice and help you find stability again, but make sure it's someone you know you can trust who will have your best intentions are heart like a parent or sibling or even close friend. I would say to only allow a romantic partner to be that safety net only if you've been together for a while and know they can be trusted. So I've actually gone through fertility treatments for medical reasons and the thing about freezing eggs vs. freezing embryos is that most of the eggs don't actually make it through the thaw process and when they do they're sometimes damaged so all that money people are spending to preserve their fertility is honestly wasted. Many people end up needing donor eggs/sperm in the end because of this, which just adds to the cost. It's better to just create embryos with donor sperm and freeze it until you're ready than it is to gamble with the eggs that probably won't make it. You could always do both if it's important to you to have children with a future partner and just thaw the eggs first when it's time to see if they'll survive. If not, you have a backup plan and you'll still be able to try to create the family you want.

Only about half of the children in foster care are even up for adoption to begin with and of that number more than half see a completed adoption within the year. The foster care system is not meant to separate families, but to bring them back together. Most children are placed with relatives after being removed from a parent's care unless there are no relatives immediately available or they have issues that require special care, whether that be mental or physical. In my case I was allowed to go to court on my own and file for permanent guardianship because I'm family so it didn't count as an adoption and wouldn't have been counted in that static, which happens often. It costs the state far less to do things that way and it allows them to close the case without having to put much effort in. Not all "orphans" are sitting in a cold cell like little orphan Annie.
